claim: 19 CFR 190.2 defines drawback as the refund, in whole or in part, of duties, taxes, and/or fees paid on imported merchandise.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: "the refund, in whole or in part, of the duties, taxes, and/or fees paid on imported merchandise."

claim: Drawback can cover ordinary customs duties, marking duties, internal revenue taxes that attach upon importation, merchandise processing fees, and harbor maintenance taxes.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: Eligible: ordinary customs duties; marking duties under section 304(c); internal revenue taxes that attach upon importation; merchandise processing fees; harbor maintenance taxes.

claim: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not subject to drawback.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: Not eligible: Antidumping and countervailing duties.

claim: Direct identification manufacturing drawback covers articles made in the United States with imported merchandise and will not exceed 99 percent of the duties, taxes, and fees paid.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: "articles manufactured or produced in the United States with the use of imported merchandise" ... "will not exceed 99 percent"

claim: Substitution manufacturing drawback requires substituted merchandise classifiable under the same 8-digit HTSUS subheading as the imported merchandise, with drawback capped at 99 percent of the lesser of two duty amounts.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: "classifiable under the same 8-digit HTSUS subheading number as the imported merchandise" ... "will not exceed 99 percent of the lesser of"

claim: For manufacturing drawback, articles must be exported or destroyed within 5 years after importation of the merchandise designated for the claim.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: "within 5 years after importation of the merchandise identified to support the claim"
verifier_note: Wording found in § 190.27(a) (direct identification) and § 190.22 ('not to exceed 5 years from the date of importation'), both on the Part 190 page.

claim: Direct identification unused merchandise drawback applies to imported merchandise exported or destroyed under CBP supervision that was not used in the United States, capped at 99 percent of duties, taxes, and fees paid.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: "has not been used within the United States before such exportation or destruction" ... "will not exceed 99 percent"

claim: Unused merchandise must be exported or destroyed within 5 years of importation and before the drawback claim is filed.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: § 190.31(b): the merchandise must be exported or destroyed within 5 years of importation and before the claim is filed.

claim: Performing operations that do not amount to manufacture or production is not treated as a use of the merchandise for unused merchandise drawback.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: § 190.31(c): performing operations that don't amount to manufacture or production does not count as a use of the merchandise.

claim: For substitution unused merchandise drawback, the substituted merchandise must be in the possession of the claimant before exportation or destruction and generally meet the 8-digit HTSUS standard.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: "in the possession of the party claiming drawback" ... "the 8-digit HTSUS substitution standard in § 190.2"

claim: Rejected merchandise drawback covers merchandise that does not conform to sample or specifications, was shipped without the consignee's consent, or has been determined to be defective as of the time of importation, at 99 percent of duties paid.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: § 190.41: "has been determined to be defective as of the time of importation" ... "will be 99 percent of the amount of duties paid"
verifier_note: Corrected by verifier-V8: § 190.41 limits the defect ground to goods defective 'as of the time of importation'; claim and page sentence/table updated, then verified against fetched text.

claim: For rejected merchandise drawback, substituted merchandise must share the same 8-digit HTSUS subheading and the same specific product identifier such as a part number, SKU, or product code.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: Rejected merchandise drawback: substitute must match the 8-digit subheading and share the same specific product identifier, such as a part number, SKU, or product code.

claim: Returned retail merchandise drawback covers imported duty-paid goods sold at retail, returned to and accepted by the importer, then exported or destroyed under CBP supervision, using an entry imported within 1 year before export or destruction.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: § 190.45: sold at retail, returned to and accepted by the importer; entry imported "within 1 year before the date of exportation or destruction."

claim: For returned retail merchandise, the claimant certifies that the designated and returned merchandise share the same 8-digit HTSUS subheading and specific product identifier, and the refund is capped at 99 percent of duties paid.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: "specific product identifier (such as part number, SKU, or product code)" ... capped at 99 percent of the duties paid

claim: The Notice of Intent to export or destroy (CBP Form 7553) must be filed at least 5 working days before intended exportation, unless another period is approved or prior notice is waived.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: "5 working days prior to the date of intended exportation"

claim: CBP decides whether to examine or waive examination within 2 working days after receiving the Notice of Intent; without timely notice, the merchandise may be exported without delay.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: "Within 2 working days after receipt of the Notice"

claim: A complete drawback claim is timely if successfully transmitted not later than 5 years after the date the designated merchandise was imported.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: "successfully transmitted not later than 5 years after the date on which the merchandise designated"

claim: A complete drawback claim includes the electronic drawback entry, applicable Form 7553 notices, applicable import entry data, and evidence of exportation or destruction.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: § 190.51(a)(1): the electronic drawback entry, applicable Form 7553 notices, applicable import entry data, and evidence of exportation or destruction under subpart G.

claim: Drawback records must be retained for 3 years after liquidation of the claims, or longer if required by law.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: "must be retained for 3 years after liquidation of such claims"

claim: Acceptable evidence of exportation includes carrier records such as ocean bills of lading and air waybills, records from a CBP-approved electronic export system, and official postal records for mail shipments.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: § 190.72(b) documents "include, but are not limited to" ocean bills of lading, air waybills ... CBP-approved electronic export system ... official postal records

claim: For goods exported by mail, official postal records describing the shipment are sufficient to prove exportation and must be identified on the drawback entry and kept in the claimant's records.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: "official postal records (original or copies) which describe the mail shipment will be sufficient to prove exportation"
verifier_note: Text is in § 190.74 (exportation by mail), within subpart G.

claim: Rejected merchandise may also be the subject of an unused merchandise drawback claim to the extent it qualifies.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: "Rejected merchandise may be the subject of an unused merchandise drawback claim"

claim: For drawback purposes, destruction means destroying articles or merchandise to the extent that they have no commercial value.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: "the destruction of articles or merchandise to the extent that they have no commercial value."

claim: The drawback regulation defines manufacture or production to include processes that make merchandise into a new and different article having a distinctive name, character or use.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: "a process, including, but not limited to, an assembly" ... "into a new and different article having a distinctive name, character or use"

claim: The refusal to pay a claim for drawback is a decision that can be protested.
publisher: Office of the Federal Register / National Archives (eCFR)
evidence: § 174.11(b)(6): "The refusal to pay a claim for drawback;"
